title: ProgNet: Program-Grounded Evidence Composition for Interpretable Graph Classification

problem.claim: Graph classification requires explanatory structures that are integrated into the prediction mechanism.

gap.claim: Existing methods generate isolated, instance-specific explanations rather than grounding reasoning in reusable structural programs.

contributions.claim: ProgNet treats explanatory structures as first-class, reusable components of graph classification.
ProgNet represents graphs with a shared vocabulary of human-interpretable programs written in a graph pattern description language.
ProgNet uses a decomposable evidence composition network that scores and aggregates program-level evidence with additive, signed logit attributions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on eight graph-classification benchmarks report competitive predictive accuracy and more faithful explanations.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper presents ProgNet as an interpretable graph-classification framework with explanatory structures integrated into prediction.
It grounds reasoning in a shared vocabulary of reusable structural programs instead of isolated instance-specific explanations.
Graphs are represented using human-interpretable programs, with a vocabulary designed for coverage, diversity, compactness, and reuse.
A decomposable evidence network produces additive signed attributions, and benchmark experiments report competitive accuracy with more faithful explanations.

source_observation.claim: A shared vocabulary of reusable structural programs is used to ground predictions in explicit structural evidence.

interpretation.claim: Reusable intermediate representations may support explanations that generalize across instances better than isolated explanations.

application.claim: For interpretable graph classification, design explanation primitives as shared, reusable program-level components.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when reusable programs outperform instance-specific explanations or how vocabulary quality affects performance.

unknowns: Benchmark identities, datasets, baselines, and quantitative results are not specified.
The faithfulness evaluation protocol and independent verification are not described.
The program language, vocabulary-construction procedure, and model-training details are omitted.
